mainTopic: Whether one person can forbid another's use through the air (אוסר דרך אויר): finding sources for שמואל and for רב
overview: The גמרא brings a ruling about a בור (cistern) four טפחים away from the walls of two courtyards. Each neighbor may draw water through his window after putting out a small זיז (ledge), and רב יהודה says even a reed is enough. אביי tells רב יוסף that this ruling follows שמואל, because רב holds that one person does not forbid another 'through the air.' The גמרא looks for a source for שמואל's view. A proof from a roof next to a רשות הרבים is pushed off using רב פפא's explanation, so the real proof is the cistern ruling itself: a ledge is needed only because, without one, each neighbor would forbid the other through the air. Then the גמרא looks for a source for רב's view. A proof from two balconies, one above the other, is pushed off because the upper balcony has easier access, like a doorway against throwing. Finally the גמרא brings רב's ruling about two houses with three ruins between them, where each house may use the ruin next to it by throwing. The ruling continues on the next amud.

steps.title: A cistern between two courtyards: each side puts out a small ledge and draws water
steps.stepSummary: A בור sits four טפחים from the wall of each of two courtyards. Each neighbor may put out a tiny זיז and then draw water from the cistern through his window.
steps.simpleTranslation: There is a cistern between two courtyards, four handbreadths from this wall and four handbreadths from that wall. This neighbor puts out a ledge of any size and draws water, and that neighbor puts out a ledge of any size and draws water.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא states a ruling about two neighbors who share access to one cistern on שבת. It tells us what each one must do in order to draw water.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The cistern is four טפחים from each wall, so neither neighbor can reach it without using the open air between. The ruling says a tiny ledge sticking out of each window is enough, and then each may draw. The ledge works like a marker that each one is drawing through his own extension.

keyTerms.meaning: A cistern or water pit
Courtyards
Set apart, at a distance from
A ledge or projection sticking out from a wall
Of any size, even the smallest amount
Draws or fills water

steps.whyThisMatters: This ruling becomes the key proof later in the sugya for שמואל's view that one person can forbid another through the air.

phrases.english: A cistern that is between two courtyards,
set four handbreadths away from this wall
and four handbreadths away from that wall —
phrases.notes: Because of this distance, reaching the cistern means using the open air

phrases.aramaic: זֶה מוֹצִיא זִיז כׇּל שֶׁהוּא וּמְמַלֵּא,
phrases.english: this one puts out a ledge of any size and draws water,

phrases.aramaic: וְזֶה מוֹצִיא זִיז כׇּל שֶׁהוּא וּמְמַלֵּא.
phrases.english: and that one puts out a ledge of any size and draws water.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the ruling under discussion from the previous part of the daf
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Each neighbor may draw from a cistern four טפחים away once he puts out a small ledge.

steps.title: רב יהודה's own view: even a reed is enough
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה, speaking for himself, says that even sticking out a simple reed is enough. A real ledge is not needed.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רב יהודה himself said: even a reed.
steps.whatsHappening: רב יהודה gives his own opinion, which is more lenient than the ruling he just reported. He says a reed sticking out is enough.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ruling in step 1 asked for a ledge. רב יהודה keeps the idea that some marker is needed but makes it easier, so a reed is enough. He still requires something, which will matter in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: His own (opinion), not quoting someone else
A reed or stick

phrases.english: And Rav Yehuda himself said:
Even a reed (is enough).

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a more lenient personal view to the ruling in step 1
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A reed sticking out is enough. A real ledge is not needed, but some marker is.

steps.title: אביי: this ruling follows שמואל, not רב
steps.stepSummary: אביי tells רב יוסף that רב יהודה's ruling follows שמואל. רב holds that one person does not forbid another through the air, so according to רב nothing at all would be needed.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said to רב יוסף: This ruling of רב יהודה follows שמואל. If it followed רב, he said: a person does not forbid his fellow through the air.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי identifies whose opinion stands behind רב יהודה's ruling. He says it must be שמואל, because it does not fit רב.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב holds that using a place only through the air does not let one neighbor forbid the other. If so, each could draw from the cistern freely, with no ledge or reed. Since רב יהודה still asks for some marker, he must be following שמואל, who holds that a person does forbid through the air.

keyTerms.meaning: An אמורא, student of רב יוסף
Forbids his fellow (makes the other's use not allowed)
By way of the air, without touching or walking there

steps.confusionAlert: Both רב and שמואל were teachers of רב יהודה. אביי is asking which of his two teachers this ruling follows.

phrases.english: Abaye said to Rav Yosef:
This ruling of Rav Yehuda follows Shmuel,
for if it followed Rav, didn't he say:
A person does not forbid his fellow
by way of the air.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Identifies the opinion behind the ruling in steps 1 and 2
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Requiring any marker only fits שמואל. רב holds there is no forbidding through the air.

steps.title: Where do we know שמואל's view from?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for the source showing that שמואל holds a person forbids his fellow through the air.
steps.simpleTranslation: And שמואל's view, from where do we know it?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks how we know that שמואל holds this view. This sets up the attempts at a proof in the next steps.
steps.deeperAnalysis: אביי assumed שמואל disagrees with רב. The גמרא wants an actual statement of שמואל that shows it.

keyTerms.meaning: From where? (What is the source?)

phrases.english: And Shmuel's view, from where (do we know it)?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the source of the view אביי gave to שמואל
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which statement of שמואל shows he holds a person forbids his fellow through the air

steps.title: First proposed source: a roof next to the public domain
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests the proof comes from שמואל's ruling that a roof next to a רשות הרבים needs a fixed ladder before the courtyard may use it.
steps.simpleTranslation: If you say from this, which רב נחמן said in the name of שמואל: A roof next to the public domain needs a fixed ladder to permit it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא offers a first possible source for שמואל's view: his ruling about a low roof beside the public domain.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The idea is that people in the רשות הרבים can use the roof through the air, for example by throwing things onto it. That would forbid the roof to the courtyard unless a fixed ladder connects it to the courtyard. If so, שמואל holds that people forbid through the air.

keyTerms.meaning: If you say (introduces a proposal that is often rejected)
Roof
Public domain
A fixed, permanent ladder

phrases.english: If you say from this
which Rav Nachman said in the name of Shmuel:
A roof next to the public domain —
needs a fixed ladder to permit it.
phrases.notes: The assumption is that the public's use through the air is what forbids it

steps.triggerLanguage: אִילֵּימָא מֵהָא דְּאָמַר רַב נַחְמָן אָמַר שְׁמוּאֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a first answer to the question in step 4
steps.raayaObject: שמואל holds a person forbids his fellow through the air
steps.raayaSupportSource: שמואל's ruling, reported by רב נחמן, that a roof next to the רשות הרבים needs a fixed ladder

steps.title: Rejected: the roof case can be explained like רב פפא
steps.stepSummary: The proof is pushed off. Maybe the roof case is like רב פפא explained: the public actually puts hats and cloaks on that roof, so it has nothing to do with the air.
steps.simpleTranslation: Perhaps it is like רב פפא!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the roof proof by giving another way to understand שמואל's roof ruling.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב פפא explained that the roof is low enough that people in the street rest their hats and cloaks on it. That is direct physical use, not use through the air. So the roof ruling proves nothing about forbidding through the air.

keyTerms.meaning: Perhaps (introduces another possible explanation)
An אמורא whose explanation of the roof case is mentioned here

phrases.english: Perhaps it is like Rav Pappa!
phrases.notes: רב פפא: the public places hats and shawls on the roof, which is direct use

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof offered in step 5
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Only the roof proof is rejected. The claim about שמואל's view still stands.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The roof case can be explained by direct physical use (hats and cloaks), not use through the air

steps.title: The real source: the cistern ruling itself
steps.stepSummary: The proof comes from the cistern ruling. A ledge is needed only because, without one, each neighbor would forbid the other through the air.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, from this: This one puts out a ledge of any size and draws, and that one puts out a ledge of any size and draws. The reason is that he put one out. But if he did not, we say a person forbids his fellow through the air.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives its real source for שמואל's view. It brings back the cistern ruling and reads it closely.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ruling allows drawing only after a ledge is put out. That means without a ledge, drawing would be forbidden. The only reason it would be forbidden is that each neighbor uses the cistern through the air and so forbids the other. That proves the ruling holds a person forbids his fellow through the air.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather (rejects the earlier suggestion and offers a new one)
The reason
He put out (the ledge)
We say

steps.whatToRemember: According to רב, a person does not forbid his fellow through the air, so no marker is needed. According to שמואל, a person does forbid through the air, so a ledge (or, for רב יהודה, a reed) is needed. The cistern ruling proves שמואל's view through the reasoning 'only because he put one out.'
steps.confusionAlert: The גמרא really repeats the cistern ruling here. It is not a new case. It is being reread to draw a proof from the word 'puts out.'

phrases.english: Rather, from this:

phrases.aramaic: זֶה מוֹצִיא זִיז כׇּל שֶׁהוּא וּמְמַלֵּא,
phrases.english: this one puts out a ledge of any size and draws water,

phrases.aramaic: וְזֶה מוֹצִיא זִיז כׇּל שֶׁהוּא וּמְמַלֵּא.
phrases.english: and that one puts out a ledge of any size and draws water.
The reason is that he put out (a ledge),
but if he did not put one out —
we say: a person forbids his fellow
by way of the air.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces the rejected roof proof with the cistern ruling as the true source
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The cistern ruling, read as 'only because he put out a ledge,' shows that שמואל holds a person forbids his fellow through the air

steps.title: What is the source for רב's view?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks where we see that רב holds a person does not forbid his fellow through the air.
steps.simpleTranslation: And where do we learn רב's opinion from?
steps.whatsHappening: Earlier we found a source for שמואל's view. Now the גמרא asks for the matching source for רב's opposite view. This question sets up the proofs that come next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 3, אביי said that according to רב nothing would be needed, because a person does not forbid his fellow through the air. Steps 4–7 proved שמואל's side. Now the גמרא turns to prove רב's side.

keyTerms.meaning: From where? (asking for a source)
The opinion of רב
By way of the air: using an area only by throwing or lowering things into it, not by walking in

phrases.english: And Rav's view, from where do we know it?
phrases.notes: Parallel to the earlier question about שמואל in step 4.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Having found שמואל's source, the גמרא now asks for רב's source.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A ruling of רב that shows a person does not forbid his fellow through the air.

steps.title: First proof: the two balconies over the water
steps.stepSummary: The proposed proof is a משנה about two balconies, one above the other, together with רב's ruling that if they are four טפחים apart, the upper balcony is permitted.
steps.simpleTranslation: If you say it comes from this: Two balconies sit over water, one above the other. A partition was made for the upper one but not for the lower one. Both are forbidden to draw water until they make an עירוב together. And רב הונא said in the name of רב: This was taught only when they are close to each other. But if they are four טפחים apart, the upper one is permitted and the lower one is forbidden.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא offers a first proof for רב. In the balcony case, when the balconies are spread apart, the upper balcony is permitted even though the lower balcony could still reach its space through the air.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When the balconies are four טפחים apart, the lower balcony can reach the upper one's area only through the air. רב still rules that the upper balcony is permitted. That suggests the lower balcony's air-access does not forbid the upper one, which matches רב's view.

keyTerms.meaning: Balconies jutting out (here, over a body of water)
A partition that permits drawing water from below
Until they make an עירוב (join together legally)
Close by, horizontally within four טפחים
Set apart by four טפחים

steps.confusionAlert: The 'four טפחים' here is a sideways distance between the balconies, not a height. Once they are that far apart, each balcony can reach the other's area only through the air.

phrases.english: If you say, from this:
Two balconies, one above the other,
they made a partition for the upper one
and did not make a partition for the lower one,
both are forbidden until they make an eruv together.
And Rav Huna said in the name of Rav:
They taught this only when it is close by,
but when it is four handbreadths away,
the upper is permitted and the lower is forbidden.
phrases.notes: The key line: the upper balcony is not forbidden by the lower one's air-access.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 8 with a first proposed source.
steps.raayaObject: רב's view that a person does not forbid his fellow through the air.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה of the two balconies, together with רב הונא quoting רב that when they are four טפחים apart the upper one is permitted.

steps.title: Pushing off the balcony proof: the upper one has easier access
steps.stepSummary: The proof is rejected. The upper balcony may be permitted because its access to the water is easier, not because air-access never forbids.
steps.simpleTranslation: Maybe it is different here. The lower balcony can use the water only by lifting the bucket up and then lowering it. The upper balcony uses it just by lowering. So this is like a case where one side uses an area by throwing and the other side uses it through a doorway.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes off the balcony proof. It offers another reason why the upper balcony wins, one that has nothing to do with the rule about air.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There is a known rule: when one courtyard reaches an area through a doorway and another reaches it only by throwing, the easier user gets it, and the harder user does not forbid him. Here the upper balcony has the easy access (just lowering), and the lower one has the hard access (lifting up, then lowering). So the upper one may be permitted because of easier access, and this case does not show that רב ignores air-access in general.

keyTerms.meaning: Perhaps it is different here
Throwing; here, hoisting the bucket up
Lowering (a bucket down on a rope)
A doorway, meaning easy, normal access

steps.confusionAlert: In this line, זריקה does not mean throwing sideways. It means the lower balcony has to hoist the bucket up to the upper level before lowering it to the water.

phrases.english: Perhaps it is different here,
since for this one (the lower) it is by hoisting and lowering,
and for that one (the upper) by lowering alone,
it is like a case where one uses it by throwing and the other through a doorway.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof offered in step 9.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Only the proof from the balcony case is rejected. רב's view itself is not challenged.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The upper balcony's permission can be explained by its easier access (the 'doorway beats throwing' rule) instead of a general rule that air-access does not forbid.

steps.title: Second proof begins: two houses with three ruins between them
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא starts a new proof from רב's ruling about two houses with three ruins between them, where each house uses the ruin next to it by throwing.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, it comes from what רב נחמן said in the name of רבה בר אבוה, quoting רב: There are two houses with three ruins between them. This one uses the ruin next to him by throwing, and that one uses the ruin next to him by throwing,
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא drops the balcony proof and begins a new source for רב. This step lays out the case, and the ruling continues past the end of this passage.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here both houses reach the ruins the same way: only by throwing. So 'doorway beats throwing' cannot explain the result, which was the weakness of the balcony proof. The proof comes from the line already stated: each house may use the ruin next to it, even though the other house could also reach that ruin through the air by throwing. So that air-access does not forbid.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather, from this (a new proof replacing the rejected one)
Ruins, open abandoned plots
The one next to him
By means of throwing (through windows), which is air-access only

phrases.english: Rather, from this:

phrases.aramaic: דְּאָמַר רַב נַחְמָן אָמַר רַבָּה בַּר אֲבוּהּ אָמַר רַב:
phrases.english: which Rav Nachman said, quoting Rabba bar Avuh, quoting Rav:
Two houses with three ruins between them.

phrases.aramaic: זֶה מִשְׁתַּמֵּשׁ בַּסָּמוּךְ שֶׁלּוֹ עַל יְדֵי זְרִיקָה,
phrases.english: This one uses the ruin adjacent to him by throwing,

phrases.aramaic: וָזֶה מִשְׁתַּמֵּשׁ בַּסָּמוּךְ שֶׁלּוֹ עַל יְדֵי זְרִיקָה,
phrases.english: and that one uses the ruin adjacent to him by throwing,
phrases.notes: The ruling continues on the next amud (about the middle ruin).

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא מֵהָא דְּאָמַר רַב נַחְמָן אָמַר רַבָּה בַּר אֲבוּהּ אָמַר רַב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces the balcony proof rejected in step 10 with a new source.
steps.raayaObject: רב's view that a person does not forbid his fellow through the air.
steps.raayaSupportSource: רב's ruling, through רב נחמן and רבה בר אבוה, about two houses with three ruins between them.
